title: VII. And In The Open Air
paragraphs: "The air is fresh, but in my apartment it isn't, not in any sense of the word. Let's walk slowly, sir. I'd be glad of your kind attention."
"I have something important to tell you too," Alyosha remarked, "only I don't know how to begin."

"Of course you must have business with me. You'd never have come to see me without some reason. Unless you've come simply to complain about the boy, which seems unlikely. And speaking of the boy—I couldn't explain it to you back there, but I'll describe that scene to you now. My tow was thicker a week ago—I mean my beard. That's the nickname they've given my beard, the schoolboys especially. Well, your brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch was dragging me by my beard—I hadn't done a thing, he was in a towering rage and happened to run into me. He hauled me out of the tavern into the marketplace; just then the boys were coming out of school, and Ilyusha with them. The moment he saw me in that state, he ran up to me. 'Father,' he cried, 'father!' He grabbed hold of me, hugged me, tried to pull me away, crying to the man attacking me, 'Let go, let go, it's my father, forgive him!'—yes, he actually cried 'forgive him.' He clutched at that hand, that very hand, in his little hands and kissed it.... I remember his little face at that moment, I haven't forgotten it and I never will!"

"I swear," cried Alyosha, "that my brother will express his deepest, most sincere regret, even if he has to go down on his knees in that very marketplace.... I'll make him do it, or he's no brother of mine!"

"Ah, so it's only a suggestion! It doesn't come from him at all, just from the generosity of your own warm heart. You should have said so from the start. No—in that case, allow me to tell you about your brother's highly chivalrous, soldierly generosity, because he did display it at the time. He stopped dragging me by the beard and let me go: 'You're an officer,' he said, 'and I'm an officer—if you can find a decent man to act as your second, send me your challenge. I'll give you satisfaction, even though you're a scoundrel.' That's what he said. A chivalrous spirit indeed! I withdrew with Ilyusha, and that scene is a family memory now, printed on Ilyusha's soul forever. No, sir, it's not for us to claim the privileges of noblemen. Judge for yourself. You've just been in our mansion—what did you see there? Three ladies, one a cripple and feeble-minded, another a cripple and hunchbacked, and the third not crippled but far too clever for her own good. She's a student, desperate to get back to Petersburg, to work for the emancipation of the Russian woman on the banks of the Neva. I won't even mention Ilyusha, he's only nine. I'm alone in the world, and if I die, what becomes of all of them? I simply ask you that. And if I challenge him and he kills me on the spot, what then? What becomes of them? And worse still, if he doesn't kill me but only cripples me—I couldn't work, but I'd still be a mouth to feed. Who would feed that mouth, and who would feed all the rest of them? Must I pull Ilyusha out of school and send him to beg in the streets? That's what challenging him to a duel would mean for me. It's foolish talk and nothing more."
"He will beg your forgiveness, he'll bow down at your feet in the middle of the marketplace," Alyosha cried again, his eyes glowing.

"I did think about prosecuting him," the captain went on, "but look at our code—could I really get much compensation for a personal injury? And then Agrafena Alexandrovna sent for me and shouted at me: 'Don't you dare dream of it! If you take him to court, I'll announce to the whole world that he beat you for your dishonesty, and then it's you who'll be prosecuted.' I call God to witness whose dishonesty it actually was, and whose orders I was acting under—wasn't it hers and Fyodor Pavlovitch's? 'And what's more,' she went on, 'I'll dismiss you for good, and you'll never earn another penny from me. I'll speak to my merchant too'—that's what she calls her old man—'and he'll dismiss you as well!' And if he dismisses me, where else could I earn anything? Those two are all I have to rely on, because your Fyodor Pavlovitch has not only stopped employing me, for other reasons, but means to use some papers I've signed to take me to court himself. So I kept quiet, and now you've seen our little retreat. But let me ask you—did Ilyusha hurt your finger badly? I didn't want to go into it back there in our mansion, in front of him."

"Yes, quite badly, and he was in a real fury. He was avenging you on me, as a Karamazov, I understand that now. But if only you'd seen how he was throwing stones at his schoolmates! It's very dangerous. They could kill him. Children are foolish. A thrown stone can crack someone's skull open."
"That's exactly what happened. He got bruised by a stone today. Not on the head, on the chest, just above the heart. He came home crying and groaning, and now he's ill."
"And you know, he attacks them first. He's bitter at them on your account. They say he stabbed a boy named Krassotkin with a penknife not long ago."
"I've heard about that too, it's dangerous. Krassotkin is an official here, we may hear more about it yet."
"I'd advise you," Alyosha went on warmly, "not to send him to school at all for a while, until he's calmer... until his anger has passed."

"Anger!" the captain repeated. "That's exactly what it is. He's a small creature, but it's a mighty anger. You don't know the whole of it, sir. Let me tell you more. Ever since that incident, all the boys have been teasing him about the 'wisp of tow.' Schoolboys are a merciless breed—individually they're angels, but together, especially at school, they're often merciless. Their teasing has stirred up a gallant spirit in Ilyusha. An ordinary boy, a weak-willed son, would have caved, felt ashamed of his father, sir, but he stood up for his father against every one of them. For his father, and for truth and justice. Because what he went through when he kissed your brother's hand and cried out, 'Forgive father, forgive him'—only God knows that, and I do, his father. Our children—not your children, but ours, the children of poor gentlemen looked down on by everyone—know what justice means, sir, even at nine years old. How could rich children know it? They never plumb such depths, not once in their lives. But at that moment in the square, when he kissed that hand, at that moment my Ilyusha grasped the whole meaning of justice. That truth entered him and crushed him forever, sir," the captain said, heated again, in a kind of frenzy, striking his right fist against his left palm as if to show how "the truth" had crushed Ilyusha. "That very day, sir, he came down with a fever and was delirious all night. All that day he'd barely said a word to me, but I noticed he kept watching me out of the corner of his eye, even though he'd turned to the window and pretended to be studying his lessons. But I could see his mind wasn't on his lessons at all. The next day I got drunk to forget my troubles, sinful man that I am, and I don't remember much. Mamma started crying too—I'm very fond of mamma—well, I spent my last kopek drowning my sorrows. Don't think less of me for that, sir—in Russia the men who drink are often the best men. The best among us are the biggest drunkards. I lay down and don't remember what happened with Ilyusha, though the boys had been jeering at him at school all that day. 'Wisp of tow,' they shouted, 'your father was dragged out of the tavern by his wisp of tow, and you ran along behind begging forgiveness.'"

"On the third day, when he came home from school, I saw he looked pale and wretched. 'What is it?' I asked. He wouldn't answer. Well, there's no talking privately in our mansion without mamma and the girls joining in. What's more, the girls had heard about it the very first day. Varvara had started snarling. 'You fools, you buffoons, can't you ever do anything sensible?' 'Quite right,' I said, 'can we ever do anything sensible?' For the moment I brushed it off like that. So that evening I took the boy out for a walk, because you should know we go walking every evening, always the same route, the one we're walking now—from our gate to that big stone lying by itself in the road, under the fence, which marks the start of the town pasture. A beautiful, lonely spot, sir. Ilyusha and I walked along hand in hand, as usual. He has a small hand, his fingers thin and cold—his chest troubles him, you know. 'Father,' he said, 'father!' 'Yes?' I said. I saw his eyes flash. 'Father, the way he treated you!' 'It can't be helped, Ilyusha,' I said. 'Don't forgive him, father, don't forgive him! At school they say he paid you ten rubles for it.' 'No, Ilyusha,' I said, 'I wouldn't take money from him for anything.' Then he started trembling all over, took my hand in both of his, and kissed it again. 'Father,' he said, 'father, challenge him to a duel—at school they say you're a coward and won't challenge him, and that you'll take ten rubles from him.' 'I can't challenge him to a duel, Ilyusha,' I answered. And I explained briefly what I've just told you. He listened. 'Father,' he said, 'still, don't forgive it. When I grow up I'll challenge him myself and kill him.' His eyes were burning, blazing. And of course, being his father, I had to say something: 'It's a sin to kill,' I said, 'even in a duel.' 'Father,' he said, 'when I grow up, I'll knock him down, knock the sword right out of his hand, I'll throw myself on him, wave my sword over him, and say: "I could kill you, but I forgive you—so there!"' You can see what's been going on in that small mind of his these last two days; he must have been plotting that revenge all day and raving about it half the night.

"But then he started coming home from school badly beaten—I found out about it the day before yesterday—and you're right, I won't send him to that school anymore. I heard he'd been standing up against the whole class alone, defying every one of them, that his heart was full of resentment, of bitterness—it worried me. We went for another walk. 'Father,' he asked, 'are rich people stronger than everyone else on earth?' 'Yes, Ilyusha,' I said, 'there's no one on earth stronger than the rich.' 'Father,' he said, 'I'll get rich, I'll become an officer and beat everyone. The Tsar will reward me, I'll come back here, and then no one will dare—' Then he fell silent, his lips still trembling. 'Father,' he said, 'what a horrible town this is.' 'Yes, Ilyusha,' I said, 'it's not a very nice town.' 'Father, let's move to another town, a nice one,' he said, 'where people don't know about us.' 'We'll move, we will, Ilyusha,' I said, 'only I need to save up for it.' I was glad to be able to steer his mind away from painful thoughts, and we started dreaming about how we'd move to another town, how we'd buy a horse and cart. 'We'll put mamma and your sisters inside, tuck them in, and we'll walk—you can ride for a bit now and then, and I'll walk alongside, because we have to spare the horse, we can't all ride at once. That's how we'll go.' He was thrilled at that, especially at the thought of having a horse and driving it. Of course a Russian boy is born loving horses. We talked on like that for a long while. Thank God, I thought, I've managed to distract him and comfort him.

"That was the evening before yesterday, but last night everything changed. He'd gone to school in the morning, came home depressed, terribly depressed. In the evening I took him by the hand and we went for our walk; he wouldn't talk. The wind was blowing, no sun, that autumn feeling in the air; twilight was coming on. We walked along, both of us gloomy. 'Well, my boy,' I said, 'what about setting off on our travels?' I was hoping to bring him back to our talk from the day before. He didn't answer, but I felt his fingers trembling in my hand. Ah, I thought, this is bad; something's happened. We'd reached the stone where we're standing now. I sat down on it. And in the sky there were kites everywhere, flapping and wheeling. As many as thirty in sight. Of course, it's just the season for kites. 'Look, Ilyusha,' I said, 'it's time we got out last year's kite again. I'll mend it—where did you put it away?' My boy said nothing. He looked away, turned sideways from me. Then a gust of wind kicked up the sand. He suddenly fell against me, threw both his little arms around my neck, and held on tight. You know how children get, when they're silent and proud and try to hold back their tears through some great trouble, and then suddenly break down—their tears come in streams. With those warm streams of tears, he suddenly soaked my face. He sobbed and shook as if he were having a fit, pressing himself against me as I sat on the stone. 'Father,' he kept crying, 'dear father, how he insulted you!' And I sobbed too. We sat there shaking in each other's arms. 'Ilyusha,' I said to him, 'Ilyusha, darling.' No one saw us then. Only God saw us, and I hope He'll count it in my favor. You should thank your brother, Alexey Fyodorovitch. No, sir, I won't thrash my boy just to satisfy you."

He had slipped back into his original tone of resentful clowning. Alyosha sensed, though, that the man trusted him, and that if someone else had been standing in Alyosha's place, the captain wouldn't have spoken so openly, wouldn't have told him what he'd just told him. This encouraged Alyosha, whose heart was trembling on the edge of tears.
"Ah, how I'd like to be friends with your boy!" he exclaimed. "If you could arrange it—"
"Certainly, sir," the captain murmured.

"But now, listen to something else entirely!" Alyosha went on. "I have a message for you. That same brother of mine, Dmitri, has also insulted his fiancée, a noble-hearted young woman you've probably heard of. I have the right to tell you about the wrong done to her; in fact, I ought to, because when she heard about the insult done to you and learned about your unfortunate situation, she instructed me at once—just now—to bring you this help from her—only from her, not from Dmitri, who has abandoned her. Not from me, his brother, either, nor from anyone else—from her, only from her! She begs you to accept her help.... You've both been insulted by the same man. She thought of you the moment she'd received a similar insult from him—similar in its cruelty, I mean. She comes to you like a sister helping a brother in trouble.... She told me to convince you to take these two hundred rubles from her, as from a sister, knowing how badly you need it. No one will ever know, it can't give rise to any unjust gossip. Here are the two hundred rubles, and I swear you must take them—unless all men on earth are meant to be enemies! But there are brothers on this earth too.... You have a generous heart... you must see that, you must," and Alyosha held out two crisp, rainbow-colored hundred-ruble notes.

They were both standing by the big stone near the fence at that moment, and there was no one nearby. The notes seemed to hit the captain like a shock. He started, but at first only from sheer astonishment. Such an outcome to their conversation was the last thing he'd expected. Nothing could have been further from his mind than help from anyone—let alone a sum like that!
He took the notes, and for a moment could barely speak, an entirely new expression crossing his face.
"That's for me? So much money—two hundred rubles! Good heavens! Why, I haven't seen that much money in the last four years! Mercy on us! And she says she's a sister.... And that's really true?"
"I swear that everything I've told you is the truth," Alyosha cried.
The captain flushed red.

"Listen, my dear friend, listen. If I take it, won't I be behaving like a scoundrel? In your eyes, Alexey Fyodorovitch, won't I be a scoundrel? No, Alexey Fyodorovitch, listen, listen," he hurried on, touching Alyosha with both hands. "You're persuading me to take it, saying it comes from a sister, but deep down, in your heart, won't you feel contempt for me if I take it, eh?"
"No, no, I swear on my salvation I won't! And no one will ever know except me—me, you, her, and one other lady, her closest friend."

"Never mind the lady! Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch, at a moment like this you need to listen, because you can't understand what these two hundred rubles mean to me right now." The poor man was working himself up, little by little, into a kind of incoherent, almost wild enthusiasm. He'd been knocked off balance and talked extremely fast, as if afraid he wouldn't be allowed to say everything he had to say.

"Besides the fact that it's honestly earned, coming from a 'sister' so deeply respected and revered—do you realize that now I can look after mamma and Nina, my hunchbacked angel of a daughter? Doctor Herzenstube came to see me, out of the kindness of his heart, and examined them both for a full hour. 'I can't make anything of it,' he said, but he prescribed a mineral water sold at a chemist's here. He said it would be sure to help her, and he ordered hot baths too, with some medicine dissolved in them. The mineral water costs thirty kopeks, and she'd need maybe forty bottles of it; so I took the prescription and laid it on the shelf under the icons, and there it's stayed. And he ordered hot baths for Nina, with something dissolved in them, morning and evening. But how can we manage a cure like that in our mansion, with no servants, no help, no bath, and no water? Nina has rheumatism all over, I don't think I mentioned that. Her whole right side aches at night, she's in agony, and would you believe it, the angel bears it without a groan, for fear of waking us. We eat whatever we can get, and she'll only take the leftovers, scraps you'd barely give a dog. 'I'm not worth it, I'm taking it from you, I'm a burden on you'—that's what her angel eyes seem to say. We wait on her, but she hates it. 'I'm a useless cripple, no good to anyone.' As if she weren't worth it, when she's the saving grace of all of us with her angelic sweetness. Without her, without her gentle voice, it would be hell in that house! She softens even Varvara. And don't judge Varvara too harshly either, she's an angel too, she's suffered wrong as well. She came to us for the summer, bringing sixteen rubles she'd earned and saved from giving lessons, meaning to go back to Petersburg with it in September—which is now. But we spent her money and lived on it, so now she has nothing to go back with. Though really she couldn't go back anyway, since she has to slave for us like a servant. She's like an overworked horse with all of us riding on her back. She waits on everyone, mends and washes, sweeps the floors, puts mamma to bed. And mamma is moody, and tearful, and out of her mind! And now, with this money, I can hire a servant, do you understand, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I can buy medicine for these dear creatures, I can send my student off to Petersburg, I can buy beef, feed them properly. Good Lord, it's like a dream!"
Alyosha was delighted that he'd brought the man such happiness, and that the poor fellow had let himself be made happy.

"Wait, Alexey Fyodorovitch, wait," the captain began, talking with a frenzied rush, swept up in a new daydream. "Do you know, Ilyusha and I might actually manage to carry out our dream after all. We'll buy a horse and cart, a black horse—he insists it has to be black—and we'll set off just as we imagined the other day. I have an old friend, a lawyer in K—— province, and I've heard from a reliable man that if I went to him, he'd give me a clerk's position in his office—so who knows, maybe he really would. I'd just put mamma and Nina in the cart, and Ilyusha could drive, and I'd walk, I'd walk alongside.... Why, if I could just manage to collect one debt that's owed me, I might have enough for that too!"

"There would be enough!" Alyosha cried. "Katerina Ivanovna will send you as much more as you need, and you know, I have money too, take whatever you need, as you would from a brother, a friend, you can pay it back later.... (You'll get rich, you'll get rich!) And you know, you couldn't have a better idea than moving to another province! It would be your salvation, especially your boy's—and you should go soon, before winter, before the cold sets in. You must write to us once you're there, and we'll always be like brothers.... No, it's not a dream!"

Alyosha could have hugged him, he was so pleased. But glancing at him, he stopped short. The man stood with his neck stretched out and his lips protruding, his face pale and frenzied. His lips were moving as though trying to form words; no sound came out, but still his lips moved. It was unsettling.
"What is it?" Alyosha asked, startled.

"Alexey Fyodorovitch... I... you," the captain muttered, stumbling over his words, staring at him with a strange, wild, fixed look, an air of desperate resolve. At the same time there was a sort of grin on his lips. "I... you, sir... wouldn't you like me to show you a little trick I know?" he murmured suddenly, in a firm, quick whisper, his voice no longer faltering.
"What trick?"
"A pretty trick," the captain whispered. His mouth twisted at the left corner, his left eye screwed shut. He kept staring at Alyosha.
"What's wrong? What trick?" Alyosha cried, thoroughly alarmed now.

"Why, look," the captain suddenly squealed, and showing him the two notes he'd been holding by one corner between thumb and forefinger throughout the conversation, he crumpled them up savagely and squeezed them tight in his right fist. "Do you see, do you see?" he shrieked, pale and furious. And suddenly flinging up his hand, he hurled the crumpled notes onto the sand. "Do you see?" he shrieked again, pointing at them. "Look there!"
And with wild fury he began stamping on them with his heel, gasping and shouting as he did:
"So much for your money! So much for your money! So much for your money! So much for your money!"
Suddenly he darted back and drew himself up in front of Alyosha, his whole frame radiating an unspeakable pride.

"Tell whoever sent you that the wisp of tow doesn't sell his honor," he cried, throwing his arm up in the air. Then he spun around and started to run; but he hadn't gone five steps before he turned completely around and blew Alyosha a kiss. He ran another five paces and then turned one last time. This time his face wasn't twisted with laughter, but shaking all over with tears. In a tearful, faltering, sobbing voice he cried:
"What would I say to my boy if I took money from you for our shame?"

And then he ran on without turning back. Alyosha watched him go, grieved beyond words. Oh, he understood now that until the very last moment the man himself hadn't known he was going to crumple up the notes and throw them away. He didn't turn back. Alyosha knew he wouldn't. He wouldn't run after him and call him back—he knew exactly why. Once the man was out of sight, Alyosha picked up the two notes. They were badly crushed and crumpled, pressed into the sand, but undamaged, and they even rustled like new ones when Alyosha unfolded them and smoothed them out. After smoothing them out, he folded them, put them in his pocket, and went to report to Katerina Ivanovna on how her errand had turned out.
